- What's the Goal of a Curiosity Gap?: Kind: captions Language: en Have you ever seen a headline online that made you feel an irresistible urge to click it, even if you knew it might be a little sensational? Perhaps it promised to reveal a secret or share something unbelievable that happened next. This powerful pull is often the work of something called a curiosity gap. The primary goal of a curiosity gap is to create an information deficit in your mind, compelling you to seek out the missing pieces. It strategically opens a question or presents an intriguing incomplete idea, making you feel an urgent need to fill in that blank. This technique is designed to immediately grab your attention and drive engagement, usually a click. This technique works so effectively because it taps into a fundamental human psychological trait. Our natural desire for cognitive closure and resolution. Our brains are wired to seek completeness. And when we encounter a gap in our knowledge, especially about something novel or emotionally charged, it creates a kind of mental itch. Content creators exploit this by providing just enough information to peique your interest and make you aware of what you do not know without giving away the full story. This triggers a mild state of suspense and anticipation, releasing doppamine and motivating you to find the answer. To recognize and respond to a curiosity gap, pay attention to headlines that are vague, overly dramatic, or pose rhetorical questions without immediate answers. They often promise astonishing revelations, hidden truths, or shocking outcomes. You can recognize them by their use of phrases like, "You will not believe what happened next, the secret, too," or, "What they do not want you to know." The goal is to make you feel as though you are missing out on vital information. Understanding the curiosity gap is an insider's view into media manipulation. It is not just about clickbait headlines, but also influences how stories are structured in news, advertising, and even social media posts. This deliberate crafting of an information deficit, sometimes referred to as information foraging, is a powerful tool used to guide your attention and behavior across various platforms, often without you even realizing it. By becoming aware of how a curiosity gap works, you can become a more discerning consumer of information. Recognizing this psychological tactic empowers you to pause and critically evaluate content rather than automatically falling prey to the urge to click. This helps you avoid misleading information and make more intentional choices about where you direct your valuable attention online. If this helps you think critically, like, [music] subscribe and stay informed with us.

- Navigating AI with curiosity and caution | Tom Janssen-Groesbeek | TEDxROC Nijmegen: Kind: captions Language: en Hi everyone, my name is Tom Fusbe. I'm a researcher at the Robot University where I work at the digital security department and my research focuses on AI security and more specifically on large language model security. And when I was a child, I spend a large amount of time playing with the computer at my parents' home. I uh I was only playing on the computer, testing what it could do, uh installing games, even when I couldn't even speak the language of English. I would just go put in the CD and press buttons until I could play the the game. And sometimes I would also break things on the computer that I didn't want my parents to know. So I just figure out how to fix it and then they wouldn't know and I could continue. And today as my role as a researcher, I'm still breaking things. Uh but actually I'm breaking AI systems to see where their boundaries are and to see how we can fix them and make them better. And during my research I already noticed that you don't really need high technical skills to break these systems. You just need language because language is all you need. Language is all you need with large language models. So if you go online with Jet GPT, Gemini, Deepseek, you can already start a simple conversation and you can do beautiful things. you can do creative things, but because we also only need language to do these uh beautiful things, there's a real security risk that the malicious actors also only need language to do bad things. So today I'm going to show you two techniques that are out there that can be used to push these models beyond their boundaries to let them do something that they shouldn't do or some harm harmful things they can do. And I'm not going to show you to scare you. I really just want to inform you that these techniques are out there that these models are still not 100% secure so that you can navigate with these models how you could use them without breaking them or how you could figure out if someone else broke it and you maybe uh can defend yourself against them. So the first technique I want to discuss is called the jailbreak. It's a technique focused on large language models uh where we push these models beyond their initial instruction. So if you're talking about a large language model, these models are trained to output the best output depending an input. So there is input sentence. Uh they have learned from the data set of text that there is patterns in these texts. They know that if there's an input sentence by or A, then the best possible output sentence is B. Uh but because of the the large amount of text that is out there, these models also learn potential harmful things to output. - Crosswalks Are Striped Because Of A 1949 British Study: Kind: captions Language: en You have walked across thousands of them in your life and you have never asked the question. A pedestrian crosswalk. White stripes painted on the asphalt perpendicular to the flow of traffic repeating in a parallel pattern across the road. Most people call them zebra crossings. The stripes have been the standard for over 70 years. But why stripes? Why not a solid white rectangle? Why not two parallel lines marking the boundary? Why not a dashed line like the lane markers on the highway? The answer is a 1949 British transportation study about how human eyes perceive contrast at night in rain on a windshield with the wipers going. Here are the reason why. Walk down any city street and look at the road. At every intersection there is a crosswalk. White paint. Parallel stripes. Each stripe about 1 to 2 ft wide set about the same distance apart repeating across the lane. Walk through London, Tokyo, Buenos Aires and Toronto and the stripes are identical. Same width, same spacing, same alignment. The pattern is so universal you have stopped noticing it. But the pattern is not arbitrary. It is the result of a 1949 British study that measured the human eye's ability to register contrast on wet asphalt at low light through a moving car's windshield. The stripes won every measurement. The story starts in post-war Britain. The country was rebuilding. Pedestrian deaths had spiked during the blackout years and continued into the 1940s as cars returned to streets. The Road Research Laboratory, a government engineering agency outside London, was asked to design a crossing that would actually save lives. They tried solid white rectangles. Drivers complained the rectangles looked like patches of road resurfacing and ignored them. They tried two parallel lines marking only the boundary. Drivers couldn't see the lines until they were already inside them. They tried a single dashed line. Pedestrians ignored it because it didn't look like a place to walk. None of the early designs reduced fatalities by enough to justify the paint. George Charlesworth a researcher at the Road Research Laboratory decided to approach the problem from human visual physiology instead of traffic engineering. He wired up a test track outside Slough with eight different crosswalk patterns. He drove cars across them in every condition that mattered. Daylight, dusk, night, rain, fog, headlights on, headlights off, wipers running. Drivers wore eye-tracking equipment that measured exactly when their eyes registered each pattern as a thing to brake for. The results were not subtle. The alternating black and white striped pattern was registered by the eye in less than 1 second from a moving car at every condition. Solid lines took two to three seconds. Dashed lines took four. The stripes won every test. And here is where the physiology gets elegant. The eye does not register objects by color or shape. It registers them by edges where contrast changes. A single white rectangle on dark asphalt has only two edges. A pair of parallel lines has four. A dashed line has more. But dashes are too small to read at speed. A zebra crosswalk has dozens of edges all spaced at frequencies the eye is sensitive to. The pattern shouts at the eye in a way that no single line ever can. The alternating pattern still works when half the stripes are obscured by mud or snow. The shape of the pattern is the message. But here's the part that turned a research finding into a global standard. Charlesworth's first real-world installation was at a single intersection in Teddington, Slough in October 1949. Pedestrian deaths at that one crossing dropped to zero in the first 6 months. The previous year had seen four fatalities at the same spot. The British government rolled the design out across England within 2 years. The European Conference of Ministers of Transport adopted the British zebra crossing as the European standard in 1953. The United Nations codified it as a global recommended pattern in the Vienna Convention in 1968. The same eight stripe pattern that George Charlesworth tested on a track outside London is now painted on every continent. The British called the design a zebra crossing because the alternating black and white stripes resembled the markings of an actual zebra. The Beatles walked across one in 1969 for the cover of Abbey Road and the spot on Abbey Road in London became a tourist destination. Tokyo's Shibuya scramble crossing is famous for its zebra stripes. New York repainted every Manhattan crosswalk to the zebra standard between 2010 and 2015 after pedestrian fatality reviews favored the pattern. Even autonomous vehicle vision systems are now trained on the zebra pattern because a self-driving car's camera responds to the same alternating edge contrast that George Charlesworth measured in a 1949 human eye. So the next time you step off a curb and walk across the white stripes of a crosswalk, remember the pattern is not aesthetic and not arbitrary. It is the result of a 1949 British study that asked one question. What does a human eye actually see at a moving distance in rain and night with the windshield half fog? The answer was a pattern of alternating black and white stripes sized at exactly the spatial frequency the visual cortex processes fastest. The crosswalk you step across every day is the most studied piece of paint on any street in the world. It is doing more work than the crosswalk light. More work than your own caution. Look at the next crosswalk you step across. The alternating white stripes you have walked through your entire life are the result of a 1949 British transportation study that asked exactly one question. What shape of paint does a human eye register fastest from a moving car windshield in rain, fog, low light and with the wipers running? Charlesworth's team tested eight patterns. Solid rectangles got mistaken for road resurfacing. Two boundary lines were invisible until you were inside them. Dashed lines didn't read as a place to walk. Only the alternating black and white striped pattern was registered by the eye in under 1 second from a moving car in every weather condition tested. The zebra pattern shouted at the visual cortex in a way that no other shape did. The 1949 finding spread across England within 2 years, became the European standard by 1953 and was codified globally by the Vienna Convention in 1968. Every crosswalk in every city you have ever lived in is the same answer to the same physiological question. The Beatles walked across one of these for an album cover. Self-driving cars are still trained to recognize them. The crosswalk is one of the quietest pieces of vision research ever painted onto an asphalt surface and you have stopped seeing it because the design works invisibly under your feet every single day of your life on the way to work. If this kind of small research finding quietly shaping your daily life story is your speed there is a whole channel of stories like it. - Why Does Clickbait Feel So Manipulative? - Media Literacy For Everyone: Kind: captions Language: en Why does clickbait feel so manipulative? Imagine scrolling through your favorite social media app and seeing a headline that makes your heart race or your curiosity spike. It promises something shocking or exciting. But when you click, the content often falls short. Why does that feeling of being tricked or pushed into clicking happen so often? Well, it all comes down to how these headlines tap into our emotions and how our brains work. Clickbait is designed to exploit our natural emotional responses. It uses feelings like curiosity, surprise, fear, or anger to make us want to click immediately. These emotions are powerful motivators that override our usual careful thinking. When we see a headline like, "You won't believe what happens next," our brain gets a little jolt of excitement or suspense. It creates a gap between what we expect and what we get, which is called the curiosity gap. That gap makes us want to click to fill in the missing piece. Most clickbait headlines also play on emotional appeals. They might make us feel like we're missing out on something important or threaten us with losing an opportunity if we don't act fast. Phrases like, "Do this now or risk losing everything create a sense of urgency and anxiety." That rush pushes us to click without stopping to think if the content is worth our time or if it's even reliable. Another trick is exaggeration or oversimplification. Clickbait often promises quick solutions or sensational revelations that don't match the actual content. When the article or video doesn't deliver what the headline hinted at, it leaves us feeling tricked or disappointed. This mismatch between expectation and reality is what makes clickbait feel so manipulative. Understanding these tactics is key to becoming a smarter media consumer. When we recognize emotional appeals and the curiosity gap, we can pause and ask ourselves if the content is really worth our attention. Developing these critical media analysis skills helps us avoid impulsive clicks driven by emotional manipulation. Instead, we can choose to engage with content that truly informs or entertains us without feeling pressured or tricked. In the end, clickbait feels manipulative because it uses our emotions and mental shortcuts to get us to click on things that often don't deliver. By learning to spot these tricks, we can navigate online content more thoughtfully and protect ourselves from feeling manipulated or deceived.

Plus, they knew that relying on other platforms to drive traffic to viral hits was risky, since those other platforms might disable the traffic at any time. And it also talks about teasers that intentionally withhold information to exploit the "curiosity gap." They give you enough information to make you curious, but not enough to satisfy that curiosity. At the other extreme, you have things that are so unsensationalized as to be dull. You could call this the dead zone. Now, here is where you would find "Strange applications of the Magnus Effect." - Is Clickbait A Threat To Journalistic News Values? - Journalism Explained: Kind: captions Language: en Is clickbait a threat to journalistic news values? Imagine clicking on a headline that promises shocking news or a secret reveal only to find something quite different. That's the world of clickbait and it raises a big question. Does it threaten the core principles that make journalism trustworthy? Clickbait uses sensational, misleading, or emotionally charged headlines to get people to click. Its main goal is to boost views, shares, and add revenue, not to inform accurately. This often means sacrificing truthfulness and depth in reporting. When headlines exaggerate or withhold key details, they create what is called a curiosity gap. Readers want to know more, but the content often falls short of expectations. This can make the audience feel tricked or disappointed, which weakens trust in new sources. Journalism is built on values like accuracy, fairness, and providing the public with reliable information that matters socially. When clickbait takes over, these values are at risk. Instead of delivering balanced stories, some outlets focus on grabbing attention with shocking or emotional headlines. This can lead to the spread of misinformation or superficial stories that don't really serve the public interest. People tend to respond strongly to headlines that evoke fear, anger, or excitement. This emotional reaction makes sharing easy, but it can also spread false or exaggerated stories quickly. Responsible journalism aims to give context and present facts clearly, not to manipulate emotions for clicks. Historically, sensationalism has existed in journalism for a long time. In the past, yellow journalism in the 19th century prioritized sensational stories over accuracy. But today, with the rise of social media and digital platforms, clickbait's reach has grown exponentially. It's easier than ever for misleading headlines to go viral, which can damage the reputation of genuine news outlets. Journalists and news organizations face a tough balancing act. They want to attract audiences in a crowded media space, but also have a duty to uphold standards of truth and relevance. Avoiding clickbait involves creating headlines that honestly reflected the story's content. This builds trust and helps the public make informed decisions. In the end, clickbait does pose a challenge to journalistic news values. It pushes some outlets to prioritize attention over accuracy. But responsible journalists can resist this trend by focusing on transparency and truthful reporting. That way they help maintain credibility and serve the public's right to honest information.

Just a few years before, I’d gotten really interested in keyword targeting and had gotten really good at ranking on YouTube and Google searches associated with poi tutorials and tricks. I started asking myself whenever I watched someone else’s video, why was I clicking on it? And I’d use the answers I’d arrive at to guide my approach with my own content. Sometimes it worked, other times it didn’t. But this project extended to my email list, too. Where before my subject lines were pretty dry but accurate descriptions of what was to be found in the full email, I started trying out different subject lines that would connect with that content, but would arouse what I keep seeing referred to as the “curiosity gap”. The curiosity gap occurs when we see a teaser for something, say a phrase, image, or snippet of video and we just have to find out more about it. It gives us just enough to want to know more without giving us the satisfaction of knowing exactly what we’re signing up for. So back to that mailing list subscriber, here…because within his rage-quitting there’s a really important piece of this puzzle to understand. So…like most people, I like to think of myself as a pretty smart guy. A 2018 paper found that 65% of American adults believe that they are of above average intelligence. On most days I’d like to think that I am, We like thinking of ourselves as smart and one of those things we associate with being smart is the capacity to verify information without bias and not to be easily manipulated. There’s no shortage of people who believe they are “too smart” to be misled. And yet… There’s a book that I really love to quote from time to time called “Thinking, Fast and Slow” by Daniel Kahneman that I legitimately think might be one of the most fascinating books I’ve ever read in my life. And one of my favorite parts of it is how it pokes holes in our conception of how smart people should be able to make smart decisions. One such example is a very famous problem: let’s say you go down to the corner store and pick up a toy baseball and a toy baseball bat. In total, you spent $1.10 and you spent a dollar more on the bat than you did the baseball. How much did you spend on each one? Now, I have given this problem to dozens of friends. Physicists, lawyers, mathematicians, teachers. And it’s wild because in presenting the problem, I can see them looking for the trick in it…they arrive almost instantly at what seems like a very clear answer and ask themselves “that can’t be it, right?” But still being drawn toward that very answer even if they’re skeptical of it. If you guessed that the bat cost $1 and the ball cost $.10, then congratulations! You gave the same answer as 80% of the people who answer this same question for the first time, including myself. And we are all wrong. The difference in cost between $1 and $.10 is $.90, not a dollar, but because we grasp onto what seem like crystal clear markers in the formulation of the problem, our brains refuse to let go of those two numbers unless under duress. The answer is actually that the bat cost $1.05 and the ball cost $.05 and it seems obnoxiously obvious in retrospect. The difference between people who opt for the first answer versus the second answer, though, isn’t a question of intelligence. It’s a question of what Kahneman refers to as system 1 versus system 2 thinking…wherein system 1 is fast, intuitive, and satisfying, system 2 is slow, difficult to parse, and frequently unpleasant to engage in precisely because it requires us to engage more of our brain’s resources in utilizing it. Okay, so why am I talking about a Behavioral Psychology problem in a video about clickbait? Because we as human beings are prone to impulse and finding quick answers to questions and many of us who pride ourselves on being smart hate being reminded that we still do this. Because really, people wouldn’t use clickbait if it didn’t work. If those titles didn’t engage the curiosity gap. If it were not easier to click on them than it would be to engage system 2 thinking. My frustration and anger is not at the author of the clickbait–it’s at myself for realizing that I was gullible enough to fall for it. And it also becomes a problem for me learning how to do it myself, because I have spent so much time resenting clickbait that I avoided learning from it. There is an art to finding a balance between creating a title that is so misleading that it will disappoint everyone versus coming up with one that does arouse the curiosity gap and also delivers real satisfaction for the viewer if they click on it. And I have to say…one of the weirdest elements of getting pushback on this is that when people complain about clickbait titles, whether they realize it or not they’re basically saying “I’m cool with you creating content just so long as you don’t actually try to get anyone to watch it.” Now, don’t get me wrong, there’s a lot of clickbait out there that does not deliver on one’s expectations…but the problem is that we are now at a point in the maturation of online content where we can’t work without it. After all, which title would you be more likely to click on: this poi trick that broke me or behind the back waistwrap combo. The latter tells you exactly what it is and because of that you’re likely to leave it for when you’re in the specific mood to watch it if you ever remember to watch it at all. Clickbait exists because in an information economy built on one of our most scarce resources, that is human attention, the ability to appeal to people was always going to be a race to the bottom. We basically have two extremes of how we engage with content: it’s either stuff that arouses our curiosity gap to crave answers so much that we can’t help ourselves to them or stuff that is so familiar, unchallenging, and predictable that it’s comforting to engage with. The latter really only works for Star Wars and MCU movies. The former is the realm of YouTube, Instagram, and Tiktok. We as content creators have to play this game or we become irrelevant. The human brain always lags behind the technology that surrounds it and we have to play catch-up for how it engages with said technology. Think about how absurd that logic is in literally any other context. We don't ban cars entirely just because some people make the terrible decision to drive drunk. If there are any limitations in any of this then this can lead to something called bias. There are many potential sources of bias in medical imaging AI. Second is during the data collection itself bias can be introduced. This is because there are many different types of imaging equipment to manufacturers. There are different techniques to acquire images and this leads to a large variation in image data. Then there can be data selection bias where the data is just from a small group of people and doesn't represent the wider population. The next step is establishing ground truth. And again, bias can be introduced at this point where there's errors or inconsistency in those annotation processes by the experts. And then the AI system itself can be biased where the model itself based on the way that it's learning and trained can actually create biases that can exacerbate through time. This has led to researchers and developers to consider the training data sets more carefully and recent developments have attempted to ensure the data sets are more representative representative of the population into which they're going to be applied. So what is highquality data and what is representative data? High quality data is accurate. It is complete and free from noise. It's related to the acquisition and the annotation of the data sets. On the other hand, and often in conflict with that is representative data which has to include diverse images from different demographics ensuring that this AMI model performs well across all population groups. Unfortunately, many data sets that are available today suffer from biases such as over representation of single groups or under representation of other groups. However, this is not easy to resolve. This is a major challenge. Data sets are impacted by access to health care both nationally, internationally and for different demographics. There are also requirements on image data sets that have to be met for them to be able to be used in im images have to be anonymized which means all patient information is removed before being used. Patients have to have consented for these images to be used to be developing AI systems. Also these um images have to be data sets that are readily available and images are very very large in in terms of data and so storage transfer all of these things are a big problem as well. Most data sets that fit these criteria actually come from clinical trials. Now these are often undertaken in certain demographical areas, certain geographical areas, sometimes in st single institutions and sometimes even just on one piece of equipment. And so here is where we have the problem. So how can we start to address this issue? Well, as I mentioned, it's not easy at all. Most images are taken for a specific clinical reason. AI development is not often in the mind of the health care professionals during a very busy medical imaging department. So this can lead to huge variation in data sets. So to address these issues, we need to focus on several key areas. First, data collection or the imaging must follow more standardized protocols and include diverse data sets. This means sourcing images from various hospitals, clinics, ensuring a mix of age, gender, ethnicity, and any other relevant factors. But consent and ethical practice is essential and often makes this hard to achieve. Secondly, data annotation by health care professionals is a is a task that has to be done properly. There has to be consistent labeling practices to ensure high levels of accuracy. But this isn't easy to do and it is time consuming task that cannot be replaced. Thirdly, robust data management has to be in place. Management systems are essential to maintain data integrity and facilitate access for AI developers. Finally, developers need to be considerate and transparent of their data sources. In summary, the key to unlocking the full potential of medical imaging AI and in way wider health care lies in the quality and diversity of the data we use to train the systems. I urge all of you to advocate for better data practices in our communities and our organizations. Together, we can build AI systems that are not only accurate, but are also fair and inclusive. Imagine a future where AI transforms health care for everyone, regardless of who they are. And as we move into this future where a AI improves outcomes for everyone, never forget that it always starts with your data. Thank you. Thank you very much. Fantastic talk. really insightful.

Yet not only can you know&nbsp; more than him about the world, you also can have a deeper&nbsp; understanding of how everything works. I'm not saying you're more intelligent than&nbsp; Aristotle or wiser. That's not the point. The point is only that science&nbsp; is cumulative, and we live later. You don't have to be a scientist. You don't have to play the Bunsen&nbsp; burner in order to understand enough&nbsp;&nbsp; science to overtake your imagined&nbsp; need and fill that fancied gap. Science needs to be released&nbsp; from the lab into the culture. It's like we've forgotten who we are... Explorers, Pioneers not Caretakers. But knowledge is preferable&nbsp; to ignorance better by far&nbsp;&nbsp; to embrace the hard truth than a reassuring faith. If we crave some cosmic purpose,&nbsp; then let us find ourselves a worthy goal. It would be very healthy for&nbsp; the human species if uh there&nbsp;&nbsp; were less discouragement and more scientists.

- What Makes A Viral Clickbait Headline Misleading? - Media Literacy For Everyone: Kind: captions Language: en What makes a viral clickbait headline misleading? Imagine scrolling through your favorite social media feed and seeing a headline that makes your heart race or your curiosity spike. But then when you click, the story doesn't quite match the hype. That's the trap of misleading clickbait headlines. They often promise something sensational but deliver something quite different. The main issue is that they overstate or distort what the article actually contains. This creates a gap between what the headline suggests and what you find when you read further. Many clickbait headlines use the curiosity gap. They hold back key details, making you wonder what's behind the story. This makes you want to click to satisfy your curiosity. But sometimes the article only gives a vague or trivial answer, which can be disappointing. It's like being promised a secret and only getting a small hint. That's why these headlines can be misleading. They raise expectations that aren't met. Another common trick is using exaggerated words like shocking, unbelievable, or worst. These words make the story seem more dramatic than it really is. They play on your emotions, making you think you're about to see something truly extraordinary. But often the story is just ordinary or not as exciting as the headline claims. This emotional manipulation can make it hard to think critically about what you're reading. Vague promises are also a red flag. Headlines that say this one trick will change your life or you won't believe what happened without explaining what the trick is or what happened are often misleading. They try to lure you in without giving real details upfront. When you click, you might find the content is shallow or not related to the headline at all. Overpromising is another key point. Headlines that promise secret tips or ultimate guides often lead to articles that are shallow or filled with generic advice. They might be sponsored content or just recycled information that doesn't really provide new or useful insights. This makes the headline a bait handswitch tactic. Many clickbait headlines also play on your emotions like fear, anger, or excitement. They want you to click because they know strong feelings make you act quickly. But this can make it harder to see through the falsehoods or exaggerations. From a media literacy view, recognizing these tactics helps you spot false or misleading headlines. Ask yourself if the headline is specific or just vague and sensational. Check if the article actually supports its claims with facts. Be aware if the headline is trying to trigger strong emotions rather than inform. And always look for reputable sources that match the story. Knowing how clickbait headlines mislead through exaggeration, vagueness, and emotional tricks helps you become a smarter consumer of online information. It keeps you from falling for false claims and helps prevent the spread of misinformation.

And the most dangerous heristic of all, which clickbait mercilessly exploits, is confirmation bias. >> The brain's desperate desire to be right. We are biologically hardwired to seek out and remember and automatically trust information that aligns with our pre-existing worldview >> and aggressively ignoring anything that challenges it. >> Right? If a headline confirms a lingering fear I have or validates a suspicion I hold about a company or a public figure, my brain bypasses the skepticism checkpoint entirely. Suddenly all the garbage makes sense. >> In traditional finance, arbitrage is the practice of exploiting price differences in different markets. You buy an asset for a dollar in market A and instantly sell it for $110 in market B, and you pocket the risk-free dime. >> Simple enough. >> Advertising arbitrage applies this exact same logic to human attention. The creators of that Julia Roberts slideshow operate as buyers in one market and sellers in another. Basically >> essentially yes the human brain operates on an energy conservation model. Processing new complex or contradictory information requires significant cognitive effort. However, when we encounter a statement repeatedly, the neurological pathways used to process it become smoother. >> And this cognitive ease is dangerous because the brain frequently misinterprets the feeling of ease for the feeling of truth. The arbitrageer provides the bait and the algorithm provides the fictionless distribution network. >> So, we have mapped the anatomy of the disease. We see how the psychology and the economics and the code all interlock to create a polluted information ecosystem. The logical question is if algorithms and machine learning created this monster by optimizing for our worst impulses, can we build better machines to slay it? >> Can technology fix the mess it created? >> Let's move into the realm of the AI counter offensive because the research paper from the Stanford University CS224N project is one of the most fascinating things in our source stack. >> The Stanford researchers asked a profoundly ambitious question. Could we architect a deep learning model capable of ingesting a piece of manipulative clickbait, looking at the sensational headline and the actual body text and automatically rewriting it into a highquality objective journalistic headline? >> They titled the project declick baiting the news. >> I love the premise. It's like trying to build a digital water filter for the internet, but the mechanics of how an AI actually writes a sentence are incredibly complex. How did they approach the architecture? They utilized a dual model framework leveraging two distinct highly advanced neural networks to essentially play a game of writer and editor. The core generator, so the model tasked with actually writing the new words was based on an architecture called T5, >> which stands for texttoext transfer transformer. I had to read up on this because the terminology is dense. T5 is what's known as an encoder decoder sequence model. Right. >> Exactly. Unlike older AI that might just try to predict the next word based on statistics, T5 is designed to take a sequence of text as an input, say an entire article, encode the semantic meaning of that text into a mathematical representation, and then decode that math back into a new sequence of text based on the specific prompt it was given. >> It reads, it compresses the meaning and it writes. >> But if you just let T5 run wild, it might read something grammatically perfect but completely false. It needs supervision. So the Stanford team brought in a second AI to act as the enforcer. >> Yes, the second model was based on the BERT architecture. Birectional encoder representations from transformers. >> It sounds like Sesame Street characters running a supercomput. >> It really does. But BERT is incredibly powerful for classification tasks. Because it reads birectionally, meaning it looks at the words before and after a target word simultaneously. It has a profound understanding of context. In this experiment, the researchers fine-tuned BERT specifically to act as a clickbait detector. >> Okay. >> Its singular purpose was to look at a headline, analyze the linguistic patterns, and assign it a clickbait score. >> So T5 is the eager junior reporter trying to write a snappy headline. And Bert is the grizzled, cynical editor sitting across the desk, ready to slap the reporter's wrist if they use too many exclamation points or dangling curiosity gaps. >> That is a brilliant analogy. Now, to train the T5 reporter to write good headlines, the researchers had to define what good actually means in mathematical terms. They established three competing objectives. Goal one was retain the author's original intent. >> They didn't want the AI to completely hallucinate a new angle. It needed to preserve the stylistic core of the original piece. >> Goal two was accurately summarize the article body. The headline must be factually anchored to the text. And goal three was eliminate clickbait phrasing entirely. Balancing those three directives seems almost impossible for a machine. I mean, human editors struggle with that. How do you actually program an AI to care about abstract concepts like intent and factual summary? >> You utilize a system of mathematical penalties known in machine learning as loss functions. >> I was fascinated by this when reading the methodology. A loss function is essentially digital pain receptor, right? It's a point system. If the AI generates an output that violates a rule, its loss score increases. The neural network is relentlessly driven to optimize its pathways to get that loss score as close to absolute zero as possible. So how did they structure the penalties? >> They implemented three distinct penalty metrics. First was the author intent loss. To measure this, they used an evaluation metric called a BLU score. Bleu essentially calculates the enagram overlap, which is the literal word for word similarity between the AI's generated headline and the human author's original headline. If the AI deviated too radically from the human's vocabulary, the BLEU score dropped, the loss function spiked, and the AI was penalized. >> Okay, so penalty one is stay true to the original words. What was next? >> Penalty two was the summarization loss. For this, they brought in yet another AI model, a summarizer called Bart, to generate a perfectly dry factual condensation of the entire article body. They then compared the AI's generated headline against this perfect summary using a metric called a rouge score which measures recall. How much of the core information was successfully captured. >> They also use something called cosign similarity to measure the semantic distance between the two texts. >> Let me pause on cosign similarity because the mechanism behind it is mindbending. The AI doesn't understand English right. It turns words into numbers. It plots every concept on a massive multi-dimensional grid. So the word apple might be plotted close to the word fruit but far away from the word car. >> Right? It's spatial >> cosign similarity measures the literal geometric angle between the headline and the summary on that massive grid. If the angle is wide, the meanings are different and the AI gets penalized. >> That is exactly how it works. It maps semantics into geometry. So that was penalty 2. Ensure the geometry of the headline matches the geometry of the facts. Do not lie. And finally they applied the classification penalty. This is where the BERT editor steps in. >> If BERT analyzed the generated text and detected the linguistic geometry of clickbait, like the emotional trigger words or the structural withholding of facts, it slammed the AI with a massive penalty. >> So, the T5 neural network is trapped in a multi-dimensional maze. It has to navigate toward an exit while satisfying three contradictory masters. Do not change the words too much, summarize all the facts perfectly, and absolutely do not sound sensational. How did the models perform under these constraints? >> This is the most compelling finding of the entire Stanford paper. Because the results were entirely counterintuitive, the researchers logically assumed that combining multiple rules, specifically stacking the summarization loss and the classification penalty together, would produce the ultimate bulletproof headline. Factually accurate and emotionally sober. >> It makes perfect logical sense. Summarize the data and don't be clickbait. The best of both worlds. >> But the empirical results demonstrated the exact opposite. The model that attempted to juggle both the summarization penalty and the classification penalty simultaneously performed significantly worse across every single evaluation metric than the models that were only trained with a single penalty. >> It achieved a lower BLEU score, a worse rouge score, and weaker cosign similarity. >> Why? Why would providing the AI with more comprehensive guidelines make it objectively stupider? The researchers hypothesized that they had inadvertently created an adversarial training environment. The rules were fundamentally fighting each other within the math. Imagine the AI generates a headline that perfectly summarizes the facts of the article, successfully minimizing the summarization penalty. >> But to achieve that accurate summary, it had to use an emotionally charged word that was prevalent in the author's original text. >> Right? The moment it uses that word, the BERT editor flags it as clickbait and the classification penalty skyrockets. It's a catch22 in the code. If it fixes the clickbait problem, it ruins the summary. If it fixes the summary, it becomes clickbait. I think of it like trying to train a dog with contradictory commands. Imagine you are in the park and you throw a stick. You yell the dog to fetch the stick, but in the exact same breath, you command the dog to sit perfectly still. >> The dog doesn't average out the commands. The dog just gets completely paralyzed by the conflicting inputs, whines, and lies down in the grass. The AI couldn't find a mathematical solution that satisfied both contradictory demands. So, the quality of the output collapsed. >> The solution space was simply too narrow. It's a profound limitation of current machine learning. However, the experiment wasn't a total failure. When the researchers stripped away the competing rules and trained a model exclusively on the classification penalty, giving it the singular command to avoid clickbait at all costs, it actually became quite effective. But to achieve that, the AI developed a highly specific, almost alien behavioral quirk. >> I absolutely love how AI models develop weird coping mechanisms to solve problems. What did it start doing? >> It developed an absolute obsession with hard statistics. Through millions of iterations, the AI learned that numbers are the mathematical antithesis of sensationalism. Numbers are dry. Numbers convey objective scale. So to avoid the clickbait penalty, the AI began aggressively scraping the body text for any numerical data and jamming it into >> For instance, they fed the model an article regarding political protests surrounding the Russian elections. A human editor might write something sensational about rage in the streets. The AI desperate to be objective generated this headline. 60,000 people across eight time zones took to the streets to back Naval's campaign. >> Wow. 60,000 people across eight time zones. That is the most granular, sober, wire service sentence imaginable. It completely strips the emotion out and replaces it with pure geography and crowd metrics. >> It does. It neutralized the hype with math. Another fascinating output occurred with an article regarding French economic indicators. A human might write economic disaster looms. The AI wrote, "The number of people actively looking for work fell.9% or 31,800 last month. >> It is functionally impossible to make a.9% drop sound like clickbait. The AI found the ultimate loophole, but it wasn't flawless, right? These models still struggle with the fluidity of human syntax. >> Far from flawless. Because the AI was blindly prioritizing the insertion of data to avoid the clickbait penalty, it often lost track of the grammatical structure of the sentence. It would hit a token limit and just abruptly terminate. One generated headline regarding regulations in India read the government's crackdown on meat shops in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh has left many >> has left many left many what unemployed hungry angry it just cuts off. >> Exactly. We don't know it ran out of space and stopped generating. >> That is hilarious. The AI accidentally invented a brand new even more maddening form of the curiosity gap purely by running out of breath mid-sentence. But jokes aside, the Stanford project provides a really clear sober reality check. Artificial intelligence is making incredible strides in natural language processing. >> We can mathematically define sensationalism and train models to recognize it, but it is not a silver bullet. >> We cannot just install a magical truth filter on our browsers and expect the algorithm to save us from the algorithms. >> The technology is a tool, not a savior, which leads to the inevitable conclusion that if the machines can't fully fix the digital ecosystem, the ultimate defense mechanism has to be human behavior. We have to change how we produce content and how we consume it. >> Let's transition into our final area of exploration which is human defenses. And I want to start by looking at this from the perspective of the creators, the businesses and the marketers. Because our source stack includes insights from corporate strategy agencies, specifically expert developments and the get smart group. And they make an argument that completely subverts everything we've talked about so far. >> They argue that relying on clickbait is actually fundamentally bad for business. How is that possible? We just spent 40 minutes detailing how arbitrageers use clickbait to print money. >> How can it be bad for a legitimate business? >> It all comes down to the qualitative difference between a click and a customer. Clickbait is the digital equivalent of empty calories. Yes, if you use a hypers sensationalized headline like this one simple hack will save your business from bankruptcy, you will undoubtedly trick a thousand users into clicking the link. your traffic metrics will spike. >> But what happens the very next second? >> The user lands on your page, realizes they've been manipulated into reading a mediocre pitch for a standard CRM software package, and they experience immediate cognitive dissonance and annoyance. What is their next physical action? >> They don't read the pitch. They immediately hammer the back button to escape. They bounce. >> Exactly. And in the modern digital economy, that bounce rate is heavily monitored and aggressively penalized by the ultimate gatekeepers, which are the search engines. The Get Smart Group outlines this dynamic perfectly. >> If a business is running pay-per-click campaigns on Google Ads and the Google algorithm detects that a massive percentage of users are clicking the ad but bouncing away from the landing page in under 3 seconds, Google interprets that as a poor user experience. >> Consequently, Google plummets your quality score. >> And the quality score isn't just a vanity metric. It dictates the financial reality of your ad campaign. When your quality score drops, Google actively punishes you by charging a higher cost per click to maintain your ad placement. The algorithm literally levies a financial tax on your business for being deceptive. >> It creates a negative ROI loop. You pay more money to acquire users who hate your brand. And brand trust is arguably the most fragile asset in the digital space. If a legitimate tech company publishes a blog post titled AI just replaced, another industry is yours. Next, they are deliberately inducing panic to drive traffic. >> When the reader clicks through and discovers the article is merely announcing a minor update to an accounting tool, the reader feels played. Trust is instantly destroyed and that user will actively ignore that brand's content in the future. >> It is a short-term metric sugar high that causes long-term structural damage. And this manipulation of trust extends beyond just the text of a headline. It bleeds into the actual visual architecture of the web pages themselves. This connects directly to the research from Adobe regarding what designers call dark patterns. >> Dark patterns are the insidious structural cousins of clickbait. While clickbait manipulates your emotions through language, dark patterns manipulate your behavior through user interface design. They are structural traps deliberately engineered to steer user actions unconsciously, often coercing users into decisions they did not intend to make. >> It's the weaponization of graphic design. Yeah. To make this concrete, let's walk through a common example. Think about the last time you booked a budget airline ticket online. You navigate through the dates, you select your seat, and you reach the final checkout screen. >> Buried in a wall of text is a tiny pre-filled check box that states, "Yes, I agree to purchase the comprehensive travel insurance for $49." >> The system opts you in by default. If you are rushing or if you simply fail to spot the tiny box and uncheck it, you have effectively purchased a product against your will. >> Or consider the pricing tiers for software services. You navigate to the subscription page. The most expensive enterprise option is glowing bright green dominating the center of the screen with a massive button. >> The basic option, which is the one you actually want, is obscured in a tiny gray low contrast font at the very bottom of the page designed to blend into the background. The design is actively suppressing your agency and forcing a specific high margin choice upon you. >> It crosses the line from persuasion into outright coercion. So if businesses need to abandon clickbait to protect their quality scores and they need to abandon dark patterns to protect their brand equity, what is the viable alternative? How do legitimate companies earn attention in a crowded ecosystem without resorting to manipulation? >> The marketing agencies advocate for a return to what they term clever copy. It requires substituting manipulation with actual substantive curiosity. Instead of relying on the fear-mongering headline, "AI just replaced another industry," the expert development source suggests a paradigm shift. >> Write a headline like, "What we learned from 10,000 CRM setups." >> Oh, that is a fantastic pivot. Let's analyze the mechanics of that. What we learned from 10,000 CRM setups still successfully deploys a curiosity gap. I am genuinely interested to know what insights are gleaned from a data set that massive. >> But instead of promising an unearned emotional shock, it promises empirical substance. Yeah. It implies authority and data. >> Exactly. It leverages curiosity without relying on deception. You tell the truth, but you frame it compellingly. You build a relationship with the reader based on the actual value of your expertise rather than relying on a cheap psychological trick to steal their click. >> Okay, so the mandate for creators is clear. Stop tricking your audience or the market, and the search algorithms will eventually bankrupt you. But what about the other side of the equation? What about you, the listener, who is currently staring down a social media feed overflowing with heartbreaking announcements and fabricated celebrity photos and hyperartisan outrage bait? >> We need cognitive armor. We need practical tools. How does the academic research from Post University suggest we build modern media literacy? For a long time, the foundational tool taught in academic media literacy programs was an evaluation framework known as the CRAAP. CR AAP. It's a pneummonic device designed to help students systematically evaluate the credibility of a source. >> Okay, let's unpack the CRA test. What are the five pillars? >> The acronym stands for currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, and purpose. Let's walk through them. Currency demands that you check the timeline. When was this information published? Has it been updated? This immediately neutralizes tactics like the Nancy Worly disinformation where a 2007 misdemeanor was recycled as breaking news in 2018. >> Relevance asks you to evaluate if the content actually addresses your needs or if it is a 40page slideshow deliberately obuscating the answer to generate ad impressions. >> Then we get to the core checks. Authority asks who actually authored this? Is it a credential journalist writing for an established institution or is it an anonymous blogger operating a site with a bizarre alpha numeric domain name? >> Accuracy asks, does the article provide verifiable evidence? Does it link to primary sources or is it just a wall of all caps text laden with exclamation points and emotional rhetoric? >> And finally, the most critical pillar, which is purpose. Why does this piece of media exist? Is the intent to objectively inform the public? Or is the design clearly engineered to induce anger, encourage viral sharing, and generate programmatic ad revenue for a hidden creator? Are there sponsored content links masquerading as news articles crowded into the footer of the page? >> I am going to push back pretty hard on this framework. I completely understand why the CRA test is a phenomenal tool for a university student sitting in a library diligently researching a 20page term paper. >> But let's look at the reality of human behavior. I am standing in my kitchen waiting for the microwave to ding and mindlessly scrolling my phone. I see a headline claiming a major theme park is shutting down. I literally do not have the cognitive bandwidth or the time to execute a rigorous five-point academic background check on the author's credentials. >> The friction is too high. If media literacy feels like a homework assignment, nobody is going to do it. How do we transform this from an academic chore into an instinctual mental reflex? That is the exact friction point that modern educators are wrestling with. The CRP test is thorough, but it is slow. It relies on what is called vertical reading, which is staying on the specific web page and scrolling down, analyzing the site's own internal architecture, reading their about us page, and trying to determine if they look legitimate, >> which is inherently flawed because a site designed to deceive you is obviously going to lie on its about us page. The camouflage is part of the grift. >> Precisely. which is why the digital literacy guidelines from Central Methodist University highlight a paradigm shift in how we evaluate information. The new standard is a technique called lateral reading popularized by the Stanford History Education Group. >> Lateral writing, how does that differ from the vertical scroll? >> Lateral reading acknowledges that the internet is an interconnected web. Instead of staying on the suspect's site and trying to decipher its internal clues, you immediately leave the site. You open a new tab horizontally or laterally and you search the broader internet to see what other established, highly trusted entities are saying about the original site or the specific claim. >> You don't ask the site if it's honest. You ask the rest of the network. >> Ah, use the power of the network against the individual bad actor. >> Exactly. And to address your concern about time lateral reading has been condensed into a rapidfire cognitive reflex known as the SIFT method, Sift. It is designed to be executed in seconds. It stands for stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, trace claims, quotes, and media to the original context. >> Let's apply Sift to the real world. I'm scrolling. I see a headline that says, "A politician was arrested and my heart rate spikes." The SIFT method kicks in. >> Step one, stop. Recognize the emotional spike. Your heightened pulse is the alarm bell that your amydala is being hacked. Pause your scroll. Do not click the share button. Step two, investigate the source. Hover over the link. Is it Reuters or is it an obscure blog called right-wing news? >> Step three, find better coverage. This is the lateral move. Open a new browser tab. Type the core claim into the search bar alongside the word Snopes or AP News. Within 5 seconds, the top result will likely be a fact check, entirely debunking the claim. >> And step four, trace claims, is exactly what we did with the buried chain. We trace the image back to an Alabama bulldozer video completely shattering the myth of the Welsh archaeological connection. >> The sift method is mental martial arts. Use the momentum of the internet to flip >> And the crucial takeaway here, which the postun university research emphasizes beautifully, is the philosophical goal behind all this education. The objective of media literacy is not to breed a society of cynics. >> That is a vital distinction. Cynicism is the easiest cognitive stance available. Cynicism is simply the blanket rejection of all information. The cynic looks at the polluted digital landscape, throws their hands up, and declares, "Everything is fake. You can't trust anything. Why bother?" >> Cynicism is a form of intellectual surrender. The goal of media literacy is to forge critical thinkers. >> And a critical thinker remains engaged. They don't reject reality. They actively evaluate it. A critical thinker encounters a shocking claim and instinctively asks the structural questions. Who manufactured this media? What are their verifiable credentials? What is the underlying financial or ideological motive driving this publication? >> They participate in the digital discourse, but they do so with their shields up. They verify before they amplify. >> They recognize that while the tools of deception are evolving rapidly, the fundamental principles of evidence and logic remain static and highly effective. >> They ensure there are actual corn flakes in the box before they pour the milk. Which brings us to the culmination of this deep dive. We've traversed a massive amount of conceptual territory today. >> We really have. We started by dismantling the psychological trles of the click, examining how a mere onetenth of a second is all the machinery needs to bypass our prefrontal cortex, flood our amydala, and exploit our inherent curiosity gaps and confirmation biases. We charted the sprawling spectrum of deception, moving from the purely financial grift of advertising arbitrageers who willingly torture reality and mash together Alabama hair tonic and Celtic history just to trap users in 53-page slideshows to the far more insidious realm of political disinformation. We saw how bad actors surgically extract tiny kernels of truth like a municipal hotline or a decade old misdemeanor and weonize them to inflame ideological divides and manipulate public perception at scale. >> We looked at the bleeding edge of the AI counter offensive analyzing how researchers at Stanford are utilizing complex neural networks like T5 and BERT to mathematically define sensationalism. >> We saw the promise of the technology but also its current limitations. how AI models can become paralyzed by contradictory rules or strip away so much emotion that they reduce the human experience to awkwardly truncated dry statistics. >> And ultimately we arrived at the understanding that while technology can attempt to build better filters, the final impenetrable line of defense resides within the human mind. We protect ourselves not through complex software but through behavioral shifts >> recognizing the emotional triggers executing lateral reading through the SIFT method and punishing deceptive corporate actors by denying them the engagement their models relied upon. >> We want to leave you the listener with a fundamental truth regarding your existence in the modern digital economy. In this ecosystem your attention is not just a metaphor. Your attention is literal liquid currency. It is the fuel that powers the servers of the arbitrageers and the algorithms of the social networks. >> Every single time you pause, take a breath, recognize a manipulative headline, and actively refuse to click, you are executing an act of defiance. You are taking power in microscopic factions of a penny out of the hands of the machine. You are starving the grifters. >> By withholding your engagement, you are demanding a higher standard of digital architecture. It is an act of quiet, powerful rebellion to simply keep scrolling. >> It is the only way the ecosystem heals. But before we sign off, I want to leave you with a brand new concept to ponder. A thought experiment built entirely upon the Stanford AI research we discussed today. The researchers successfully demonstrated that an AI can be trained to aggressively strip the sensationalism out of language and replace it with objective mathematical data. >> Rage in the streets becomes 60,000 people across eight time zones. >> The complete neutralization of the emotional hook, >> right? So extrapolate that capability 5 or 10 years into the future. - O que é Clickbait e por que ele funciona: Kind: captions Language: en-US What is clickbait and why does it work? Have you ever clicked on a video or article because the title seemed irresistible, but upon opening it, realized the content wasn't exactly what it promised? This is the infamous clickbait. The term comes from English and literally means "clickbait." It's a strategy used to attract attention and generate curiosity, leading the audience to click on a link, video, or post. Typically, clickbait uses catchy, exaggerated, or mysterious titles, often accompanied by striking images, to pique curiosity. For example: "You won't believe what happened next!" or "See the secret they don't want you to find out!" The main goal is simple: to increase the number of clicks, views, or visits to a piece of content. This can generate more engagement and, in the case of monetized websites and channels, more revenue. But not all clickbait is necessarily bad. There's ethical clickbait, where the title is attractive and arouses curiosity, but the content actually delivers what it promises. Misleading clickbait, on the other hand, exaggerates or distorts reality, making the audience feel deceived, which can damage the creator's credibility. The success of clickbait is explained by human psychology: our brains are naturally curious and seek to close "information gaps," a phenomenon called the curiosity gap. When we see something intriguing, we feel an almost automatic urge to find out more. In today's world, where the competition for attention is intense, clickbait has become a powerful tool. But the challenge is to balance attraction and honesty, so that the curiosity it sparks doesn't turn into frustration. So, the next time you come across an exaggerated headline, ask yourself: "Is it worth the click, or is it just a digital trap?"

เดือนแต่ผมก็ไม่ได้รับมัน ผมหาผู้ร่วมทุน 30 ถึง 40 คน ทุกคนตอบว่า "ไม่" ลืมมันไปซะ ผู้คนมากมายบอกว่า อาลิบาบา เป็นรูปแบบที่ห่วยมากๆ แต่ผมพูดว่า ผมเชื่อมัน และวันนึงมันจะเติบใหญ่ได้ - Ethical dilemma: Who should you believe? - Alex Worsnip: Kind: captions Language: en You’re sitting on the couch watching TV, when you hear a knock on the door. The police have just arrived to arrest your spouse— for murder. This accusation comes as a total shock. In your experience, your partner has always been gentle and loving, and you can't imagine them committing a grisly murder. But the evidence is serious: their fingerprints were found on the murder weapon. Your spouse insists they're innocent. “I know it looks bad,” they say, “but you have to believe me! If you don’t, who will?” Should you believe your spouse, even though the evidence against them looks damning? Take a second to think what you would believe in this situation. This dilemma is part of what philosophers call the ethics of belief: a field of study that explores how we ought to form beliefs, and whether we have ethical duties to believe certain things. The question here isn't about what you should do, such as whether or not you should find your spouse guilty in a court of law. After all, you wouldn’t be on the jury in their trial! Rather, it’s about what you should believe to be true. So, what factors should you consider? Perhaps the most obvious is your evidence. After all, to believe something is to take it to be true. And evidence is, by definition, all information that helps us determine what's true. From this, some philosophers draw the conclusion that evidence is the only thing that ought to determine what you believe. This view is called evidentialism, and a strict evidentialist would say it doesn’t matter that the accused is your spouse. You should evaluate the evidence from a neutral, objective point of view. Taking the perspective of an unbiased third party, your judgment of your spouse's character is a relevant consideration. But finding their fingerprints at the crime scene is surely stronger evidence. So, from an evidentialist point of view, you should either believe your spouse is guilty, or at best remain undecided. Some philosophers present evidentialism only as a view of what’s most rational to believe. But others, like 19th century evidentialist W.K. Clifford, think that following the evidence is also morally required. One argument for this view is that having well-informed, accurate beliefs is often vitally important to determining the ethical way to act. Another argument is that there’s something unethical about being dishonest, and refusing to follow the evidence is a way of being dishonest with oneself. However, perhaps there are other ethical factors in play. Although the evidence against your spouse is strong, there’s still a chance that they’re actually innocent. Think for a moment about how it would feel to be innocent, and have no one believe you— not even your own partner! By not trusting your spouse, you run the risk of seriously hurting them in their crucial hour of need. Moreover, consider what this lack of trust would do to your marriage. It would be incredibly difficult to continue a loving relationship with someone that you believed— or even strongly suspected— was a murderer. You might try to pretend to believe that your spouse is innocent, but could you really go on living that lie? According to a theory of the ethics of belief called pragmatism, these kinds of practical considerations can sometimes make it right to believe something even without strong evidence. Some pragmatists would even say that you morally owe it to your spouse to believe them. But is it even possible to believe your spouse is innocent just because you think it’ll be good for your relationship? Or because you think you owe it to the accused? You might desperately want to believe they’re innocent, but can you control your beliefs in the same way you control your actions? It seems like you can’t just believe whatever you like when the truth is staring you in the face. But on the other hand, recall your spouse’s plea. When we say things like this, we seem to be assuming that it is possible to control our beliefs in some way. So what do you think? Can you control what beliefs you have? And if so, what will you believe about your spouse?

  5. @skyler4377: notes in case you completely procrastinated ur assignment:

scientific distortion- corruption of knowledge
-this occurs when there are ethical lapses, especially in research

ethical lapses can be small and ‘inconsequential’ in the beginning
ex. a scientist saying they won’t ask a question out of fear it’ll create a negative result that may hinder future commercialization of a product or future funding of a study

ethical lapses include self-censorship, cherry-picking questions (only choosing the ones that back up their claims/have a positive impact on their research)

these compromises and accumulation of these lapses create a ‘broader system of knowledge’ due to information distortion and generate an overall lack of trust among research/researchers

ex. we trust that drinking from plastic water bottles is safe due to the funding of research. research funded by the water bottle industry says they are 100% safe while non-funded researchers conclude there may be cause for concern regarding human safety


*why does this happen?* 
people can create sympathies for certain industries, creating more leniency and willingness to turn a blind eye to parts of research. 

-typically, the studies are not inaccurate because they’re done poorly, but because they are selective. “they might be experts, but they are not independent experts”

ex1. those who evaluate drugs and vote on approval may have financial conflicts regarding that drug- influencing their opinion 


ex2. regarding the economic crash of 2008, when asked why nobody noticed the crisis despite being so major, top economics professors stated that everyone relied on somebody else in the hopes that they were doing the right thing

*are we personally immune to bias? no.*
-a lack of independence can distort the production of knowledge. it is difficult to maintain integrity due to the difficulty of rationalizing ethical lapses daily

ex. despite the alarming rates of deaths from car accidents and mobile devices, many of us will continue to use our phones while driving as we believe it doesn’t make a personal difference to our driving

*conclusion*
we should be aware of potential bias that funded research can result in, and recognize how this can limit our knowledge over time. to combat this we need to gain a critical eye when it comes to research and value scientific integrity
